new_statements.rule_in_words: Tshobdun is not a tone language (checked syllables are high-level, unchecked high-falling, allophonically). Word prominence is a lexical pitch accent: an H-L pitch drop within the phonological word. Each stem is lexically either unaccented (default; equivalent to accent on the stem-final syllable, since suffixes are low-pitched) or carries a marked accent, and the marked accent can only sit on the penult of the stem. At most one accent per phonological word; unaccented word-initial syllables and post-accent syllables are low, everything else high (falling word-finally). Compounds take the accent of the last element. Accent is thus a binary, lexically specified choice between stem-final (unmarked) and stem-penult (marked), not a positional or weight-based stress rule; the earlier Sun 1994 description says the same thing in terms of ultimate (default) vs penultimate accent, with rare antepenultimate accents in conjugated verb forms.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned; the source states that at most one accent (H-L drop) is permitted per well-formed phonological word (p. 5).
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllabic words contrast in latent accent although their citation pitch is identical (high falling): 'pa 'pig' > ɐ́-pa 'my pig' vs ŋe 'cow' > ɐ-ŋé 'my cow' (p. 5). Accented enclitics (ergative-instrumental ='kə, locative ='ta) place their accent on the host's final syllable unless the host already has an accent (p. 6). Accent adjustment is grammatical: vocatives are marked by accent (§3.4.1, p. 14) and polar questions are formed by accenting the verb form / adding accented ə́- (ex. 31, p. 26); Sun 1994 §2.4.5 (pp. 44-45) describes this as leftward accent shift to the penult, or to the antepenult if the penult is already accented; Sun 1994 p. 38 also notes infrequent antepenultimate and pre-antepenultimate accents in conjugated verb forms and accent-retaining prefixes (futurity, imperative). A few lexical items have exceptional falling pitch on -t syllables (xtə̂t 'be short', ⁿbêt 'be low').
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (stem plus prefixes and suffixes); enclitics are treated as phrase-level extensions with their own accented/unaccented behaviour. Citation forms of monosyllables neutralize the accent contrast; it surfaces only when a prefix (e.g. possessive ɐ-) is added. Data represent the native speech of co-author Bstan'dzin Blogros (Tshobdun/Caodeng township, Ma'erkang county); the 2003 chapter and 1994 article are from Gaqiuli village, Caodeng.
new_statements.identity_note: Tshobdun = Caodeng (草登) Rgyalrong, the Caodeng subdialect of 'Sidaba' (northwestern) Rgyalrong; all three sources are by the same fieldworker (Jackson T.-S. Sun) on the same variety (Gaqiuli village / speech of Bstan'dzin Blogros, Caodeng township, Ma'erkang county, Sichuan). The sister subdialect Showu/Shawu (Glottolog's separate Zbu language) is explicitly contrasted as having a two-way level vs falling tone contrast on all syllable types, so its accent facts must not be conflated with Tshobdun's.

sources.note: §2 Phonology, p. 491: 'Caodeng phonology is characterized further by a functionally more substantial system of pitch accent in which a pitch drop (H-L) inside a phonological word plays a distinctive role.. Stem-final accent (the default situation) is in effect the same as lack of accent, as suffixes are generally low-pitched. As a matter of fact, the only position in which a marked accent occurs in this language turns out to be the penult of the stem.' Monosyllables contrast in latent accent (yser' 'gold' vs rgul 'silver').
